# Advanced Journey With Ada: A Flight In Progress
**Authors**: Gustavo A. Hoffmann, Robert A. Duff — AdaCore, CC BY-SA 4.0 | **Pages**: ~1,026 | **Chapters**: 19 | **Generated**: 2026-08-24

## Core Frameworks & Mental Models

**Types encode requirements.** Declare numeric types from the algorithm's required range/digits/delta rather than using predefined types — Ada rejects unsupportable declarations at compile time, which *is* the portability guarantee. Keep objects definite and parameters indefinite (constraints resolve at the call site). Compute intermediates in `'Base` and clamp before narrowing (saturation). Constants shared across types stay untyped named numbers (infinite-precision, compile-time).

**Views are contracts.** A partial view may understate but never overstate the full view. Use `(<>)` unknown discriminants to force clients through constructor functions; `limited private` to make copying a compile-time error wherever objects have identity (access components, locks, files, tasks). Since Ada 2005, limited aggregates, constructor functions, and extended return statements build in place — limited types keep full initialization convenience with a no-copy guarantee.

**Discriminants + variant parts encode valid states.** Per-object constants become discriminants; shape variants become `case`-on-discriminant regions, making inactive-variant access impossible. Defaults on all discriminants give runtime-mutable variants; guard discriminant-changing assignments with `'Constrained`.

**Full coverage is a maintenance tool.** Named record aggregates force a compile-time revisit of every construction site when a component is added — `others` quietly destroys that guarantee. Ada 2022 adds `[…]` container/array aggregates, iterated component associations (`[for I in R => f(I)]`), delta aggregates (copy-with-changes), and `'Reduce` folds (seed with the identity element, use a wide accumulator).

**Representation is declarative.** Enumeration codes, sizes, packed layouts, per-bit record fields: the compiler generates all bit manipulation and *rejects impossible layouts at compile time*. Keep external formats on derived types, convert explicitly at I/O boundaries (RM 13.6), and probe external bit patterns with `'Valid`. `'Object_Size` (allocated) ≠ `'Size` (minimum).

**Shared-memory control is declarative too.** `Volatile` forces every access to memory; `Independent` guarantees storage-unit addressability; `Atomic` makes whole-object access single-instruction (implies both); Ada 2022 `Full_Access_Only` forbids partial-width register access. Prefer `System.Atomic_Operations` — Exchange spinlocks, `Compare_And_Exchange` lazy init, `Fetch_And_Add` lock-free counters — over hand-rolled locking.

**Parameter passing is decided by type category, not mode.** Elementary → copy; tagged/explicitly-limited → reference; the rest is the compiler's choice — never write code that depends on the mechanism of an unspecified-category type. Overload resolution is deliberately "not too smart": disambiguate with qualified expressions `Type'(…)`.

**The four-rung error ladder.** Design failures to land as high as possible: compiler-rejected → runtime-checked → bounded error → erroneous execution. `pragma Suppress` is an efficiency-only permission whose misuse drops a safe failure to erroneous. Checks that must survive release builds use the `Ada.Assertions.Assert` procedure, not the policy-controlled pragma.

**Access types are lifetime-checked handles.** Accessibility rules compare the nesting levels of access *types* to statically ban dangling references. Default to named access types; anonymous access is for access parameters/discriminants, tagged primitives, C interfacing, and nested-subprogram callbacks — never for owning heap memory (no pool control, no Unchecked_Deallocation). Encapsulate: access type hidden in a limited private ADT, every `Free` inside `Finalize`.

**Controlled types are Ada's RAII.** `A := B` means Finalize(A), bit-copy, Adjust(A) — deep copy belongs in Adjust, release in idempotent, exception-free Finalize (implicit-call exceptions become Program_Error; the optimizer may elide calls).

**Visibility is a dial.** Set it to the narrowest position that compiles: `with` → `private with` → body-only → `limited with` (cycle-breaking via incomplete views + anonymous access). Subsystem internals go in private child packages — externally un-with-able by construction. Prefer `use type`/`use all type` over broad `use`.

**Strings by role.** `Wide_Wide_String` for symbol-accurate processing, UTF-8 for storage/transport, `Encode`/`Decode` at boundaries (GNAT: `-gnatW8` for UTF-8 sources). Ada 2022 gives every type `'Image`, customizable via the `Put_Image` aspect.

# WORLDLINE

WORLDLINE gives the working machine a branch operator. It captures the state of directories
the user nominates (that capture is **PRIME**), forks PRIME into isolated **worlds**, runs a
coding agent inside each world where it cannot reach the real files, measures what each world
actually produced, and commits exactly one world back into PRIME through a single atomic
filesystem exchange that a formally proved kernel authorized.

The mental model that keeps operation correct: **a world is a proposal, PRIME is the only
reality, and the proved kernel is the only thing that can turn a proposal into reality.** If
authorization fails or anything moved underneath it, PRIME is unchanged. Refusal is the
designed outcome, not an error to route around.

> Documented against **worldline 1.0.0**, status schema **1**. Run `worldline status --json`
> first and trust the live output over this file. Human-facing long-form docs live at
> `~/Documents/WORLDLINE-Whitepaper.pdf` and `~/Documents/WORLDLINE-User-Manual.pdf`; this
> skill is the operator's copy and is self-sufficient.

## Orient before acting

```bash
systemctl --user is-active worldlined.service   # expect: active
worldline status --json                         # PRIME, worlds, jobs, capabilities
worldline root list --json                      # what WORLDLINE owns, and the primary root
worldline adapters --json                       # which agents are usable right now
```

`prime: null` with empty `worlds` is the healthy uninitialized state: the daemon runs and owns
nothing. Do not treat it as a fault, and do not "fix" it by registering a root on your own
initiative — see the authorization contract below.

| | |
|---|---|
| Client / daemon | `~/.local/bin/worldline`, `~/.local/bin/worldlined` |
| Proved kernel | `~/.local/lib/worldline/libworldline_core.so` + `proof-manifest.json` |
| Data (payloads, overlays, live mapping) | `~/.local/share/worldline` |
| State (SQLite, events, receipts, backups) | `~/.local/state/worldline` |
| Runtime (socket, `status.json`) | `$XDG_RUNTIME_DIR/worldline` |
| Global config | `~/.config/worldline/config.json` (owner-only, or it is rejected) |
| Project config | `<primary-root>/.worldline.json` |
| Source of truth for behavior | `~/Projects/worldline` |

## Authorization contract

This is the part that matters when running WORLDLINE on someone's behalf. Three tiers:

**Run freely, no permission needed — read-only.**
`status`, `list`, `show`, `graph`, `log [--verify]`, `why`, `inspect`, `watch`, `doctor`,
`adapters`, `root list`, `shell` (inside a world), `switch`. None of these touch the user's
files or spend money. Use them liberally; they are how you ground every claim you make.

**Ask first — spends the user's model quota.**
`fork`, `race`, `ghost run`, `ghost enable`. Each one invokes an external model with the
user's credentials. Confirm the mission text, the agent(s), and that they want it started
now. A race is three concurrent agents, so it is roughly triple the spend of a fork; say so.
Never enable ghosts on your own — enabling means every future PRIME checkpoint silently forks
four speculative worlds that all call a model.

**Ask first, at the point of risk — moves or replaces the user's real files.**
`init`, `root add`, `root remove`, `collapse`, `return`. Registration relocates a directory
into the WORLDLINE store and leaves a symlink; collapse and return replace live state. Always
run the read-only prepare step, show the exact printed facts (roots, delta, conflicts,
contamination), and let the user say yes to *that specific change*. Then pass `--yes` for that
one invocation. Do not pre-emptively add `--yes` to make a script tidy — the confirmation is
the only place a human sees what is about to happen.

Everything a world's agent does is already contained: it writes to its own overlay, the host
copy is a read-only lower layer, and the only route back is an authorized collapse. That
containment is what makes running agents unattended reasonable — it is not a reason to skip
the confirmations above, which exist for the *commit*, not the exploration.

`simulate` sits in the free tier for host safety (nothing on the host changes) but the command
runs as namespace root inside the future, so echo back the exact argv before running anything
destructive-looking, the same way you would for any consequential command.

## The operating loop

Assume the user has said: *"get an agent to do X in my project, then show me and put it in if
it's good."* That is the common case and this is the loop.

1. **Confirm the ground.** `worldline root list --json`. If the project is not a managed root,
   stop and ask — registration moves their directory (tier 3). If nothing is registered at all,
   explain that one `worldline init <path>` is the prerequisite and get explicit consent.
2. **Check the evidence rig.** Read `<primary-root>/.worldline.json`. No checks declared means
   every candidate finalizes with `UNASSESSED` evidence and risk cannot drop below `MEDIUM`, so
   "is it good?" will be unanswerable. Offer to add build/test checks first — that is usually
   the highest-value five minutes in the whole workflow. See `reference/configuration.md`.
3. **Pick the agent and confirm the spend.** `worldline adapters --json` shows what is
   installed and `AVAILABLE`. One approach → `fork`. Comparing approaches → `race` with exactly
   three agents.
4. **Start it.** Prefer async (no `--wait`) for real work and poll, so a long agent run cannot
   wedge the turn:
   ```bash
   worldline fork alpha --mission-text 'Add retry with backoff to the upload path' -- codex
   worldline status --json | jq '{jobs, worlds: [.worlds[] | {alias, state}]}'
   ```
   Use `--wait` only for short or fixture runs where streaming progress is genuinely useful.

   proves *what* was applied, not that the user is happy with it.
9. **Offer the exit.** If they dislike the result, `worldline return` restores the previous
   reality through the same atomic mechanism. Mention it exists; do not run it unasked.

```

init ROOT... [--primary P] [--kind repo|config|filesystem] [--yes]
root add ROOT... | root remove ROOT | root list
```

## When something refuses

Read the code, not the vibe. Common ones: `DAEMON_UNAVAILABLE` (restart the user unit),
`NO_PRIME` (nothing registered), `NO_MISSION` (none of the four routes supplied),
`CONFIRMATION_REQUIRED` (non-interactive without `--yes`), `CONFLICT` (collapse denied —
inspect the decision and conflicts), `INVALID_CANDIDATE` (not `VALID`),
`PRIME_CHANGED_DURING_CAPTURE` (an outside writer touched a managed root mid-hash),
`ADAPTER_UNAVAILABLE` / `ADAPTER_AUTH_UNAVAILABLE` (binary or credential file missing),
`GHOSTS_DISABLED`, `SYSTEM_ROOT_COLLAPSE_UNSUPPORTED` (expected on ext4).

Full symptom → cause → action table, plus the collapse decision codes and what each one
proves about the attempt: **`reference/diagnostics.md`**.

- **`scripts/pick_candidate.py`** — rank terminal candidates from `worldline list --json` or a
  `status.json` and print a defensible recommendation with the facts behind it. Hard-filters
  anything not `VALID`, anything with conflicts or contamination, and anything with a failed
  required check; refuses to recommend at all when evidence is `UNASSESSED`, because a
  comparison with no evidence is not a comparison. Use it after a race instead of judging by

- **`scripts/health_check.sh`** — 26 assertions across a complete init → fork → collapse →

These are the ones that cost the user something real if broken.

1. **Never commit without authorization.** `collapse` and `return` need the facts screen shown
   and a yes for that specific change. No batching, no "while I'm here".
2. **Never register a root on your own initiative.** It relocates their directory.
3. **Never enable ghosts unasked**, and never start a fork or race without confirming the
   spend.
4. **Never work around a refusal.** No manual copies out of payloads, no editing a candidate to
   make it collapsible, no retrying on a weaker path to obtain some result.
5. **Never claim what you did not observe.** Read `show`, `log`, `doctor` output and quote it.

# Chapter 19: Controlled Types

## Core Idea
Controlled types — derived from `Ada.Finalization.Controlled` or `Ada.Finalization.Limited_Controlled` — hook into an object's lifetime so you can run code at creation (`Initialize`), after copy (`Adjust`), and at destruction (`Finalize`), making them Ada's mechanism for RAII-style resource management (deep copies, automatic deallocation, auto-closing files). RM reference throughout: "Assignment and Finalization" (RM 7.6) and "Completion and Finalization" (RM 7.6.1).

## Frameworks Introduced

### Initialize / Adjust / Finalize lifecycle
The three overridable procedures of a controlled type, each taking `E : in out T`.
- **What**: `Initialize (A)` is called right after object A is created (after all default initialization of its subcomponents); `Finalize (A)` is called right before A is actually finalized (scope exit, `Unchecked_Deallocation`, or overwrite by assignment); `Adjust (A)` is called right after a copy has been performed onto A.
- **When to use**: whenever a type owns a resource (heap data, file handle, lock, ID) that must be acquired at creation, duplicated or fixed up on copy, and released at destruction.
- **How**:
  1. In the private part, complete the type as `new Ada.Finalization.Controlled with record ... end record` (the type must be tagged; typically the partial view is `tagged private`).
  2. Declare `overriding procedure Initialize/Adjust/Finalize (E : in out T)` — usually in the private part so clients cannot call them explicitly.
  3. Implement acquire logic in `Initialize`, deep-copy/fix-up logic in `Adjust`, release logic in `Finalize`. Make `Finalize` idempotent (e.g. test `S.Data /= null` before `Free`).
- **Why it works / failure mode**: the compiler inserts the calls at every creation, assignment, and finalization point, so the resource protocol cannot be forgotten by clients. Failure modes: (a) an unused controlled object may be optimized away entirely — Initialize/Finalize are then never called, so never rely on their side effects; (b) `A := A;` may be skipped entirely, and anonymous objects may be elided, so Adjust/Finalize may not be called where you expect — "use Adjust and Finalize solely for their intended purposes; don't implement extraneous side-effects"; (c) an exception in an implicit Adjust/Finalize call becomes `Program_Error` (bounded error).

### Assignment semantics of controlled objects
`A := B;` on a nonlimited controlled type expands to: (1) `Finalize (A)` — the old A gets a last chance to release what it holds; (2) bit-wise copy of B's data into A; (3) `Adjust (A)` — fix up the freshly copied value.
- **When to use** (this model): whenever reasoning about what runs on assignment, and when implementing deep copy — a plain assignment is a shallow copy that duplicates access values, so `Adjust` is where you allocate new objects and copy the dereferenced data.
- **How** (RM anonymous-object model): the RM describes assignment via an anonymous object — `Anon_Obj := B; Adjust (Anon_Obj); Finalize (A); A := Anon_Obj; Finalize (Anon_Obj);`. The compiler may optimize the anonymous object away, may rename `Anon_Obj` as the new A and destroy the old one, and is *required* to build in place in some cases (e.g. initializing a constant with an aggregate `(Ada.Finalization.Controlled with ...)`).
- **Why it works / failure mode**: `Finalize` before the copy prevents leaking whatever the target held; `Adjust` after the copy repairs sharing introduced by the bit-wise copy. Failure mode: counting on an exact call sequence — the compiler's permitted optimizations (in-place building, skipping `A := A`) change which calls happen.

### Limited controlled types (`Limited_Controlled`)
Same as `Controlled` but with no `Adjust`, because limited types forbid assignment.
- **When to use**: when the resource must never be duplicated (tasks as components, file handles, unique ownership). A component of a task type *forces* the enclosing controlled type to be limited.
- **How**: derive from `Ada.Finalization.Limited_Controlled`; override only `Initialize` and `Finalize`. To force construction through a function, declare the partial view with unknown discriminants — `type Logger (<>) is limited private;` — and provide an `Init` function using an extended return.

### Encapsulating access types (unbounded stack pattern)
- **When to use**: any type whose representation is heap-allocated and must grow/shrink or be deep-copied safely.
- **How**: store an access-to-array component; allocate the initial chunk in `Initialize`; deep-copy the array in `Adjust` (allocate a duplicate, copy valid elements); `Free` (an `Ada.Unchecked_Deallocation` instantiation) in `Finalize`, guarded against `null`. "No incorrect pointer usage or memory leak can happen when we use this strategy."

### Encapsulating file handling (logger pattern)
- **When to use**: a file (or similar handle) that must be open exactly while an object is in scope.
- **How**: `Limited_Controlled` with a `File_Type` component; `(<>)` partial view forcing an `Init (Filename)` constructor that `Create`s the file inside an extended return; `Finalize` calls `Close` if `Is_Open`. Alternative: a `Filename : access String` discriminant lets `Initialize` open the file (a string discriminant is impossible — indefinite subtypes can't be discriminants), at the cost of an aliased string at the call site.

## Key Concepts
- **Lifetime of an object** — creation in the declarative part, use in the sequence of statements, finalization when scope ends; controlled types insert `Initialize` after creation and `Finalize` before destruction.
- **Default initialization vs. controlled** — record default initialization is guaranteed, needs nothing from the client, and is cheap at run time compared to controlled types; prefer it when it suffices.
- **Subcomponent initialization order** — subcomponents (default-initialized and controlled ones) are initialized *before* the enclosing type's `Initialize`; in principle "Initialize and other initialization operations are done in an arbitrary order" (RM).
- **Access-discriminant components** — a component with an access discriminant constrained by a per-object expression gets `Initialize` *after* all components without such discriminants, in declaration order (RM rule).
- **Task activation** — "for an allocator, any task activations follow all calls on Initialize": a task component activates only after the whole object is initialized.
- **Finalization order** — the exact reverse of initialization: enclosing object's `Finalize` first, then access-discriminant components in reverse declaration order, then remaining subcomponents in reverse order.
- **Normal vs. abnormal completion** — a subprogram finishing its last statement completes normally and finalization runs; an exception or abort causes abnormal completion. Objects already elaborated are still finalized before a raised exception propagates.
- **Bounded error in Adjust/Finalize** — an exception in an *implicitly* called `Adjust` or `Finalize` is a bounded error; if detected, `Program_Error` replaces the original exception. An *explicit* call propagates the original exception normally; an exception in `Initialize` is not a bounded error (and `Finalize` is then never called for that object).
- **Finalization via unchecked deallocation** — `Free (A)` calls `Finalize (A.all)` right before the memory is deallocated; the object will not be finalized again at scope end.

- Think of `Initialize`/`Finalize` as constructor/destructor and `Adjust` as the copy-fix-up half of a copy constructor: assignment = destroy old target, bit-copy, adjust copy. ## Anti-patterns
- **Side effects in Initialize/Adjust/Finalize beyond resource management** — the compiler may optimize objects out, skip `A := A`, or build in place, so extraneous effects (logging counts, global state) may silently never execute.
- **Raising exceptions from Adjust or Finalize** — an implicit call turns any exception into `Program_Error` ("finalize/adjust raised exception"), losing the original; design these procedures to avoid exceptions entirely, especially when `Initialize` allocates memory.
- **Assuming leak-free behavior on exceptions during initialization** — when a bounded error occurs mid-initialization, the compiler is *permitted but not required* to finalize already-initialized subcomponents (RM 7.6.1 Implementation Permissions); don't depend on it.
- **Reaching for controlled types when default initialization suffices** — record default initialization is guaranteed, client-transparent, and cheap; controlled types carry non-negligible run-time overhead.
- **Non-idempotent Finalize** — assignment finalizes the target, and explicit calls or repeated finalization are possible; guard releases (e.g. `if S.Data /= null`).

The ID-tracking example makes the assignment machinery observable. Type `T` is `Controlled` with an `Id : Positive` component; a protected object `Id_Gen` hands out unique IDs. `Initialize` assigns a fresh ID; `Adjust` saves `Prev_Id := E.Id`, then assigns a fresh ID; `Finalize` prints the ID being destroyed.

## Key Concepts
- **Bounded error** — an undetectable error whose possible effects the RM enumerates (often raising `Program_Error` or `Constraint_Error`).
- **Erroneous execution** — an undetectable error with nondeterministic, unbounded effects; the RM makes no promise.
- **Invalid representation** — an object's bits don't represent a value of its subtype (e.g. uninitialized); evaluating it is a bounded error (RM 13.9.1).
- **Assertion_Error** — the `Ada.Assertions` exception raised by failed asserts and contract checks.
- **Discriminant check** — verifies matching discriminants on assignment and that an accessed variant component exists for the current discriminant.
- **Elaboration check** — verifies a subprogram body (or protected entry / task activation) has been elaborated before call; defeatable via renaming-as-body tricks.
- **Renaming-as-body** — providing a subprogram body by a renames clause, which satisfies the compiler but can still fail the elaboration check at runtime.
- **Exception_Occurrence** — the value carrying name, message, and (with `-E` binding) traceback; copyable with `Save_Occurrence`, streamable with `'Read`/`'Write`.
- **By-copy parameter passing** — elementary types are passed by copy, so an exception before normal return means `out`/`in out` actuals are never updated (RM 6.4.1(17)).
- **Optimization permissions (RM 11.6)** — for predefined exceptions the compiler has flexibility about whether globals assigned near the raise point were actually updated.

## Mental Models
- Think of the four error categories as a ladder of shrinking guarantees: compiler rejects → runtime raises → RM bounds the damage → anything can happen. Design so failures live as high on the ladder as possible.
- Think of `pragma Suppress` as *permission to remove*, never a command — and of relying on removal as writing erroneous-execution-by-appointment.
- Use the procedure `Ada.Assertions.Assert` when the check must fire regardless of policy; use `pragma Assert` when the policy (`-gnata` vs. default `Ignore`) should decide.
- Think of an `out` parameter of an elementary type as a value mailed on *normal return only*: raise an exception mid-procedure and the caller keeps the old value.
